headline: Maine's 2026 Election: Where the Races Stand as Campaign Season Intensifies
body:
With 78 days until the November general election, Maine's three major statewide races are taking shape as candidates prepare for a series of debates and campaign events across the state. New polling and voter registration data released this week provide the clearest picture yet of where the races stand.

In the 2nd Congressional District, former Governor Paul LePage has opened a 7-point lead over Democratic opponent Matt Dunlap, according to a poll released Tuesday by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center. LePage leads Dunlap 48 percent to 41 percent, with 11 percent of voters undecided. The poll surveyed 712 likely voters in the district and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.7 percentage points. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report moved the race from "Likely Republican" to "Lean Republican" following the poll's release. LePage is performing strongly among rural voters and men, while Dunlap's support is concentrated in the Bangor area and college towns. Dunlap's campaign is working to boost turnout in Aroostook and Washington counties, where the candidate underperformed in the June primary. The two candidates will face off in their first debate August 21 at the Bangor Civic Center.

In Maine's U.S. Senate race, incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins is running against Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger and former state Senate majority leader from Allagash. Collins released a digital advertising campaign this week accusing Jackson of "selling out" Maine loggers by supporting environmental regulations that Collins says would harm the timber industry. Jackson called the ads a "desperate lie" and pointed to his record fighting Canadian logging trucks while serving in the state Senate. Jackson received the endorsement of the Maine AFL-CIO on Tuesday. The union represents roughly 40,000 workers across the state. Jackson is launching a "Rural Maine Bus Tour" on August 23 with stops in Millinocket, Houlton, and Presque Isle. Collins and Jackson will debate August 28 at Maine Public Television studios in Portland. Women voters, who make up the majority of Maine's electorate, are expected to be decisive in the race.

Maine's gubernatorial race is also underway, though polling remains sparse. Governor Janet Mills, a Democrat first elected in 2018 and reelected in 2022, is term-limited and cannot seek reelection. The Democratic primary was won by Attorney General Aaron Frey, who defeated former state Representative Maeve Maloney in June. The Republican primary was won by Bangor-area businessman David Boyer, who ran unsuccessfully for the Senate in 2024. Boyer, a political newcomer, has focused his campaign on economic development and energy policy. Frey, a former assistant attorney general, has emphasized healthcare and education spending. The race is expected to tighten as the general election approaches.

New voter registration data released this week by the Maine Secretary of State's office shows Republicans gaining ground heading into the fall. Since May, Republican registration has increased by 3,891 voters, compared to a gain of 2,104 for Democrats. Independents remain the largest voting bloc in the state with 398,572 registered voters, followed by Democrats with 376,421 and Republicans with 340,218. The total number of registered voters in Maine is 1,143,092.

In the state Legislature, lawmakers are preparing to return to Augusta for a vote on LD 2041, the Lewiston memorial bill, scheduled for August 26. The bill, which passed unanimously out of the Joint Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs on August 18, would allocate $500,000 for a permanent memorial and mental health resource center at the site of the 2023 Lewiston shooting. Legislative leadership in both parties has indicated the bill will pass.

Key dates in the coming weeks include the LePage-Dunlap debate on August 21, Jackson's Rural Maine Bus Tour launching August 23, the Lewiston memorial vote on August 26, and the Collins-Jackson debate on August 28.
